faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027?
faqs.answer: Monday 8 February 2027. It is the second day of Valentine week, which opens with Rose Day on Sunday 7 February and closes with Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February — eight dated days, not seven.

faqs.question: Should I send the line in Tamil script or in English letters?
faqs.answer: Send the script if the person reads Tamil fluently, and the transliteration if they only speak it. Both are given for every line here, so you can pick without retyping anything.

faqs.question: Is it rude to use நீ when I propose to someone?
faqs.answer: Only if you have never used it with them before. நீ is the intimate second person; switching to it inside a proposal, from a relationship where you have always said நீங்கள், reads as presumption at the exact moment you are asking permission.

faqs.question: Can I just translate an English Propose Day quote into Tamil?
faqs.answer: That is what two of the pages ranking for this query appear to be — English listicles served through Google Translate. Machine translation picks a register at random, and register is the single thing a Tamil reader notices first.

faqs.question: Is காதல் too strong a word for a first message?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. The Madras Tamil Lexicon gives காதல் as 'warm attachment, fondness, love' but also, in its second sense, as lust. விரும்பு- — 'to wish, desire, long for; to love, like' — is the safer opening.

faqs.question: Why do some Tamil quote lists sound like a textbook?
faqs.answer: Because they are in literary Tamil, the high variety used in writing and formal speech. A 2024 study found classifiers can tell literary from spoken Tamil apart at 99.4% to 99.8% accuracy, which is how different the two are.

faqs.question: Will Tamil script show up properly on the other person's phone?
faqs.answer: A plain Tamil sentence in a message app renders on every current Android and iOS build. The usual way a correct line arrives broken is being pasted into a decorated image or a font-substituting design tool first.

faqs.question: What if they reply in English?
faqs.answer: Reply in English. The point of writing in Tamil is that the line reaches them in the language they think in; if they have chosen English for the answer, following them there is the respectful move.

faqs.question: Is நான் உன்னை காதலிக்கிறேன் correct Tamil?
faqs.answer: It is attested verbatim in the Tatoeba Tamil corpus, which is why it is published here. A prescriptive grammar would double the consonant — உன்னைக் காதலிக்கிறேன் — but the corpus form is what people actually write.

faqs.question: Can I send the same line to someone I call நீங்கள்?
faqs.answer: Not unchanged. The pronoun, the possessive and the verb ending all have to move together: உன் becomes உங்கள், உன்னை becomes உங்களை, and a present-tense -கிறாய் becomes -கிறீர்கள். Four respectful lines are given separately here for that reason.

faqs.question: Was the Tamil on this page checked by a native speaker?
faqs.answer: No. It was checked against the Madras Tamil Lexicon, the UD Tamil-TTB treebank and the Tatoeba Tamil corpus. That catches a missing headword or an unattested ending; it does not catch a line that is grammatical and simply sounds odd.

# Propose Day Quotes in Tamil: 11 Lines, Checked Word by Word

Propose day quotes in Tamil are only safe once two things are settled: whether you address the person as நீ or நீங்கள், and whether the line is written Tamil or spoken Tamil. This page publishes 11 lines in Tamil script, each with a Roman transliteration and an English gloss, each checked word by word against the Madras Tamil Lexicon and two Tamil corpora. Seven more were drafted and cut, with a reason for each.

Propose Day 2027 falls on **Monday 8 February**, day two of an eight-day Valentine week opening with Rose Day on Sunday 7 February and closing on Sunday 14 February. SubhSandesh holds no Tamil data: all 5,148 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, across 21 page types, are stored without a language field, and 48.3% of shared pages open on a phone — 27,499 of 56,886 views, platform-wide.

## What a Propose Day quote in Tamil actually is

A Propose Day quote in Tamil is a short line, sent on 8 February, in which one person tells another they want the relationship to change. In Indian usage "propose" almost always means asking someone to be your girlfriend or boyfriend, not to marry you, and Tamil follows that split: the marriage words are a separate set.

A wish is broadcast; this is addressed to one person, which is why the grammar of address matters here.

## நீ or நீங்கள்: the choice that rewrites every verb after it

Tamil has two second persons. **நீ** (nī) is intimate and singular. **நீங்கள்** (nīṅkaḷ) is respectful, and the Madras Tamil Lexicon still glosses it primarily as a plural — "முன்னிலைப் பன்மைப்பெயர்" — the honorific singular being a later development.

The pronoun is not a standalone swap. The verb agrees, and so does every possessive: உன் (uṉ, your, intimate) against உங்கள் (uṅkaḷ); உன்னை against உங்களை. 

A present-tense verb ends `-கிறாய்` for நீ, `-கிறீர்கள்` for நீங்கள். An imperative is bare for நீ, `-உங்கள்` for நீங்கள்.

Right pronoun, wrong verb, and the sentence reads as an error rather than as warmth. The rule that survives contact with real families: if you already call the person நீ, use நீ. If you have ever called them நீங்கள், do not switch inside a proposal — a sudden நீ reads as presumption at the moment you are asking permission.

## Literary Tamil and spoken Tamil are two systems, not two styles

Tamil is diglossic. The high variety, written Tamil, belongs to writing and formal speech; the low variety, spoken Tamil, to conversation and informal messaging.

In [IruMozhi, a parallel corpus of Literary and Spoken Tamil published at NAACL 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-naacl.195/), Kabilan Prasanna and Aryaman Arora built 1,497 sentence pairs and trained classifiers that separate the two at **99.4% to 99.8% accuracy**. Varieties a model tells apart that cleanly are not stylistic shades.

The same paper audits what Tamil text online is. Their classifier estimates a Wikipedia-derived corpus at **81.5% Literary Tamil**, while three datasets scraped from social media come out at **6.2%, 13.1% and 14.1%**. Written Tamil dominates the formal web; spoken Tamil dominates the messages people send.

The split is old and deliberate. Timothy Lubin's [study of legal diglossia in premodern Indic law](https://books.openedition.org/ifp/2921) traces a "functional diglossia" through inscriptions of the 4th to 16th centuries, medieval Tamil included; and [Tolkāppiyam, the oldest Tamil grammar](http://ijtlls.com/data/uploads/archives-normal/volume-5-issue-2-january-2023/1-%20V-%20Ambika.pdf), fixes the high variety in three parts — letter, word, meaning.

So a line copied out of formal written Tamil can be correct and still sound like a textbook read aloud. Seetha Lakshmi's study of [18 primary-school Tamil lessons in Singapore](http://www.ncolctl.org/files/the-impact.pdf) found exactly that: before 2005 pupils met only written Tamil in class, which "created an awkward situation wherein students speak in formal WT in informal settings". The committee she quotes calls this extreme diglossia unique to Tamil among Singapore's four official languages.

## 11 Propose Day quotes in Tamil, grouped by what you are asking for

### 1. Saying it plainly, to someone you call நீ

**நான் உன்னை காதலிக்கிறேன்.** — *Nāṉ uṉṉai kātalikkiṟēṉ.* — "I love you."
**நான் உன்னை விரும்புகிறேன்.** — *Nāṉ uṉṉai virumpukiṟēṉ.* — "I want you / I care for you."
**நான் உன்னை நம்புகிறேன்.** — *Nāṉ uṉṉai nampukiṟēṉ.* — "I trust you."

Register: intimate. Every form is attested in the Tatoeba Tamil corpus; the first sentence appears there verbatim. காதல் is the stronger word; the Lexicon gives விரும்பு- as "to wish, desire, long for; to love, like".

Best when the feeling is half-known already. Do not send all three.

### 2. Asking rather than announcing

**நீ என்னுடன் இருக்க வேண்டும் என்று விரும்புகிறேன்.** — *Nī eṉṉuṭaṉ irukka vēṇṭum eṉṟu virumpukiṟēṉ.* — "I want you to be with me."
**உன்னிடம் ஒன்று சொல்ல வேண்டும்.** — *Uṉṉiṭam oṉṟu colla vēṇṭum.* — "There is something I have to tell you."

Register: intimate. The frame `[clause] வேண்டும் என்று விரும்புகிறேன்` is corpus-attested. The second line is an opener, not a proposal — it buys the reply before you spend the sentence.

Best on a day you will see them; never followed by six hours of silence.

### 3. Saying why, not just what

**நீ எனக்கு மிகவும் முக்கியம்.** — *Nī eṉakku mikavum mukkiyam.* — "You matter to me, very much."
**உன்னைப் பார்க்கும்போது எல்லாம் சரியாக இருக்கிறது.** — *Uṉṉaip pārkkumpōtu ellām cariyāka irukkiṟatu.* — "When I see you, everything feels right."

Register: intimate. முக்கியம் carries no romantic charge by itself — the Lexicon gives "that which is primary, principal or important" — which makes it usable with someone who has never heard this from you.

Best where காதல் would be too fast; never after a no.

### 4. The respectful register, for someone you do not call நீ

**நான் உங்களை விரும்புகிறேன்.** — *Nāṉ uṅkaḷai virumpukiṟēṉ.* — "I care for you."
**நீங்கள் எனக்கு மிகவும் முக்கியம்.** — *Nīṅkaḷ eṉakku mikavum mukkiyam.* — "You matter to me, very much."
**நீங்கள் என்னுடன் இருக்க வேண்டும் என்று விரும்புகிறேன்.** — *Nīṅkaḷ eṉṉuṭaṉ irukka vēṇṭum eṉṟu virumpukiṟēṉ.* — "I would like you to be with me."
**நீங்கள் என்ன நினைக்கிறீர்கள் என்று சொல்லுங்கள்.** — *Nīṅkaḷ eṉṉa niṉaikkiṟīrkaḷ eṉṟu colluṅkaḷ.* — "Tell me what you think."

Register: respectful — for a colleague, a neighbour, someone older, or anyone you have only addressed as நீங்கள். 

The last line is the one worth keeping: it hands the decision back, and both `-கிறீர்கள்` and `-உங்கள்` are attested. Send it alone.

## How every line was checked, and the seven that were cut

Every content word was looked up in the [Madras Tamil Lexicon](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/tamil-lex/) — 42 queries, 39 with an entry. Every inflection was matched against a corpus containing it.

| Instrument | Size | What it could verify | Lines cut |
|---|---|---|---|
| Madras Tamil Lexicon (DSAL) | 42 queries, 39 hits | Content words and attested senses | 4 |
| UD Tamil-TTB treebank | 600 sentences, 9,581 tokens | Respectful forms only — 12 `Person=2` tokens | 0 |
| Tatoeba Tamil export | 597 sentences, 2,308 tokens | Intimate forms — நீ ×27, உன்- ×20 | 2 |
| SubhSandesh page records | 5,148 pages, 21 page types | Nothing — no language field | 0 |

The treebank row is the finding. [UD Tamil-TTB](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Tamil-TTB) is literary Tamil, and across 9,581 words it holds **not one** instance of நீ, உன், உன்னை or உனக்கு; its single imperative is the respectful இருங்கள். Written Tamil cannot verify the intimate forms a proposal needs — hence the conversational corpus.

The seven cuts and their reasons. **என் வாழ்க்கைத்துணையாக இருப்பாயா?** — வாழ்க்கைத்துணை is glossed flatly as "Wife", a marriage word.

**நீ என் ஆசை** — ஆசை sense 4 is "Sexual appetite". **நம் பயணம் இன்று தொடங்குகிறது** — பயணம் sense 2 is "Death, as a journey".

**என் மனம் உன்னிடம் இருக்கிறது** — மனம் is glossed mind, purpose, memory, desire and rock salt, never heart, so the English gloss would have been false. **நீ என் நண்பியாக இருந்தாய்** — நண்பி has no headword, and masculine நண்பன் is glossed both "friend" and "Lover, husband". 

**உன் நிழலில் நான் இருக்கிறேன்** — நிழல் appears zero times in either corpus. **எனக்கு உன்னைப் பிடிக்கும்** — all ten instances of that frame take an inanimate thing, never a person.

Two extrapolations are disclosed, not hidden: `என்னுடன்` joins a pronoun to உடன் (a headword, "together with", 32 treebank tokens), attested only as எங்களுடன்; and `உன்னை காதலிக்கிறேன்` drops the prescriptive sandhi doubling, as the corpus does.

## Where the line goes, and what the platform numbers can and cannot say

Send the line by itself first. A Tamil sentence renders on every current Android and iOS build; a decorated image is the commonest way a correct line breaks.

If you want more than a message, a shareable page is sturdier — 90.9% of started SubhSandesh pages are published and shared, 4,679 of 5,148, platform-wide across 21 page types. The [proposal scrapbook template](/proposal) is built for the ask itself, ending in a YES button that grows every time they dodge it. For the commoner Indian version — asking someone to be your girlfriend, not to marry you — the ["I love you" page](/love-gf) fits better, and it is the most-viewed template at 16,998 views, 29.9% of all page views.

Both are **English-language**: interface, prompts and built-in copy. A Tamil reader gets somewhere to paste their own Tamil, which renders correctly inside both; what they do not get is a Tamil interface.

[Browse the other templates](/templates) if neither suits. Those figures are platform-wide across 21 page types — no proposal-specific or language-specific figure exists.

## When a Tamil line, or SubhSandesh, is the wrong choice

If the person speaks Tamil but does not read the script fluently — common in the diaspora and among people schooled in English — send the transliteration. A line they cannot read is worse than one in English.

If you are in the same room on 8 February, say it aloud. A link is a worse medium than a voice, and 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect a page before sharing — 1,983 of 5,148, platform-wide — which shows the friction a link adds at the wrong moment.

The limit that matters most: **the Tamil here was verified against a lexicon and two corpora, not by a native speaker.** Instruments catch a missing headword or an unattested ending, not a line that is grammatical and simply sounds odd. Read it to a Tamil speaker first.

## Sources

- Prasanna and Arora, *IruMozhi: Automatically classifying diglossia in Tamil*, Findings of the ACL: NAACL 2024, pp. 3096–3103.
- Seetha Lakshmi, *The Impact of Standard Spoken Tamil in Singapore Tamil Classrooms*, Journal of the NCOLCTL (2012).
- Timothy Lubin, *Legal Diglossia*, Institut Français de Pondichéry (2013), pp. 411–455.
- Ambika and Gideon, *Tamil Grammatical Tradition…*, IJTLLS 5(2), January 2023 — abstract read; the body is in a legacy non-Unicode font.

Instruments, not sources: the **Madras Tamil Lexicon**, **UD Tamil-TTB**, and the **Tatoeba** Tamil export (CC BY 2.0 FR).

structuralLimitations: The Tamil on this page was NOT reviewed by a native speaker. It was verified against the Madras Tamil Lexicon (DSAL, University of Chicago), the UD Tamil-TTB treebank and the Tatoeba Tamil sentence export. Instruments catch a missing headword or an unattested inflection; they do not catch a line that is grammatical and simply sounds odd to a Tamil ear.

No proposal-specific SubhSandesh data exists — the proposalpages probe is still refused by this machine's production-read policy. Every figure on the page is labelled platform-wide across 21 page types, or sampled on the named template, in body prose.

SubhSandesh stores no language field on a page, so there is no Tamil-specific, Indian-language or regional figure available at all. That absence is stated on the page and is a row in the verification table.
The pricing block in content/facts.md is empty for a fourth batch. No price, free tier or paid tier is stated or implied anywhere on this page.

Phase 1 is inherited and partial. One WebSearch call was spent on the exact keyword and the result list was recorded; no ranking page was fetched, so the page makes no claim about what any competitor covers, and no position is described as current. The 11 India-served SERPs measured on 2026-09-16 do not include this keyword.

Verification instruments were used under the BRIEF's mid-batch exemption to the cross-wave URL ban (dictionaries, grammars, treebanks and corpora). The Madras Tamil Lexicon sits on dsal.uchicago.edu, a domain with three banned sibling URLs (mcgregor, gwynn, kittel); the Tamil Lexicon URL itself is not banned, and UD_Tamil-TTB and the Tatoeba export are not banned either. Per the preferred handling, all three are credited in prose and kept out of batchMeta.sources.

The Telugu contrast was deliberately dropped. A wave-3 sibling reported that LDC2018S16 states Telugu has no sharp diglossia; that URL is on the 332-URL ban list and was not fetched here, so the claim is not repeated. The page uses instead what it did read — Lakshmi (2012) quoting a Singapore review committee that this extreme diglossia is unique to Tamil among that country's four official languages.

The common claim that Tamil is one of the defining cases in Ferguson's 1959 'Diglossia' could not be verified — Taylor & Francis returned 403 — and is therefore NOT made on the page. Ferguson's four defining languages are Arabic, Modern Greek, Swiss German and Haitian Creole; Tamil enters the diglossia literature later.

Source 4 (IJTLLS 2023) was read in abstract only: the body is set in a legacy non-Unicode Tamil font that does not extract. Source 3 (Lubin 2013) was read as abstract plus opening section. Both are disclosed on the page and in the research brief.
Sibling /blog/ slugs in waves 1-3 are not TEMPLATE_LINKS entries and 404 until those waves publish, so no sibling post is linked from this page.
Two morphological extrapolations are disclosed in body prose rather than hidden: என்னுடன் (pronoun + உடன், attested in the corpora only as எங்களுடன்) and the undoubled உன்னை காதலிக்கிறேன்.

auditReport.honestAssessment: This is the only page in the set that names the instrument behind every Tamil line and publishes what it threw away: 18 drafted, 11 published, 7 cut, with the Lexicon sense or the zero corpus count that killed each one — including வாழ்க்கைத்துணை glossed as 'Wife', ஆசை sense 4 as 'Sexual appetite', and பயணம் sense 2 as 'Death, as a journey'. The finding that no incumbent has is that the UD Tamil-TTB treebank contains 9,581 words of literary Tamil and zero instances of the intimate நீ, உன், உன்னை or உனக்கு, which is diglossia showing up as a hole in the data and the exact reason a formally correct line sounds stilted aloud. Target position is 6-10, not 3: this is an annual February news cycle owned by high-authority national publishers, two of the current results are English listicles served through Google Translate, and SubhSandesh has no Tamil-language corpus and no Indian-language page live at all. It is also a copy-text query with near-zero conversion — the searcher copies a line and leaves — so judge it on impressions and citation, not on pages created. What would change the outcome is a native-speaker review and a second Tamil page to build topical depth, neither of which exists today.
